title: They never told you that the first thing sin touches isn’t your body… it’s your vision.
paragraphs: They never told you that the first thing sin touches isn’t your body… it’s your vision.

It starts quiet. A look that lingers a little too long. A conversation that feels harmless but carries weight. A desire that whispers instead of shouts. And suddenly, something sacred begins to feel… negotiable.
This is where most people misunderstand God.
They think His boundaries around sex are about control.
But what if they’re actually about protection?
What if what God is guarding isn’t just your purity… but your identity, your future, your soul?
Because long before culture redefined intimacy, God had already defined it in a way that reveals His heart.

In the beginning, before shame ever existed, before hiding became instinct, before brokenness entered the bloodstream of humanity, Scripture records something almost too holy for our modern ears to fully grasp:

“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים… וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
(Vayihyu shneihem arummim… velo yitboshashu)
—Genesis 2:25
“They were both naked… and were not ashamed.”
No fear. No comparison. No insecurity. No performance.
Just complete exposure… without the terror of rejection.
That’s what sex was designed to live inside of.
Not performance. Not validation. Not escape.
Covenant.
Because just a few verses before, God establishes something that culture keeps trying to imitate but never quite gets right:

“וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ… וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
(Vedavaq be’ishto… vehayu levasar echad)
—Genesis 2:24
“And he shall cling to his wife… and they shall become one flesh.”
That word “דָבַק” (davaq) doesn’t mean casual attachment.
It means to cling, to cleave, to bond so deeply that separation tears something real.
Sex was never meant to be recreational.
It was meant to be covenantal.
Because something happens when bodies unite that souls cannot pretend didn’t occur.
The New Testament carries this same weight forward. Paul writes with urgency, almost pleading:
—1 Corinthians 6:16
“Do you not know that the one who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her?”
That word “κολλώμενος” (kollōmenos)… it echoes the Hebrew “davaq.”
To glue. To bond. To unite.
This is not casual language.
This is spiritual surgery.
Because sex doesn’t just involve bodies… it binds souls.
And when that binding happens outside of covenant, it creates a kind of tearing that people feel but don’t always understand.
That’s why you can “move on”… but still feel attached.
That’s why you can say “it didn’t mean anything”… but your heart refuses to agree.
That’s why something inside you feels fragmented, even when you try to act whole.
God isn’t trying to restrict pleasure.
He’s protecting unity.
Because unity without covenant becomes vulnerability without covering.
And vulnerability without covering leads to shame.
And shame is exactly what entered the story the moment sin touched intimacy.

“וַתִּפָּקַחְנָה עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם… וַיִּתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
(Vatipaqachna einei shneihem… vayitboshashu)
—Genesis 3:7
“Then the eyes of both were opened… and they knew they were naked.”
Same nakedness.
Different reality.
Because covenant had been broken.
And now, instead of safety, exposure felt dangerous.
So they covered themselves.
Just like we still do.
With jokes.
With detachment.
With pretending it didn’t matter.
With calling it “just physical.”
But your soul knows.
It always knew.
And maybe that’s why this hits deeper than you expected.
Because if you’re honest… there are pieces of you still tied to moments you wish you could undo.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because here’s the truth most people never tell you:
God didn’t design marriage to limit sex.
He designed sex to reveal marriage.
Marriage is not a contract.
It’s a covenant that mirrors Christ and His Church.

“οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν… τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν”
—Ephesians 5:31–32
“The two shall become one flesh… this mystery is profound.”
Profound.
Sacred.
Unbreakable.
Because when God protects sex within marriage, He is protecting a living picture of the Gospel itself.
A love that doesn’t leave when things get hard.
A commitment that doesn’t collapse when feelings fluctuate.
A union that says, “I see all of you… and I’m not going anywhere.”
That’s what your soul was built for.
Not temporary closeness.
But permanent covering.
And maybe you’re reading this thinking, “I’ve already crossed that line.”
So did the woman at the well.
Five relationships deep… still searching.
Still thirsty.
Still carrying something she couldn’t fix.
Until she met Jesus.
He didn’t expose her to shame her.
He revealed her to heal her.

“λέγει αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς… ἐγώ εἰμι”
—John 4:26
“Jesus said to her… I am He.”
Not “I was.”
Not “I might be.”
“I AM.”
The One who restores what’s been fragmented.
The One who redeems what’s been misused.
The One who doesn’t just forgive your past… He rewrites your future.
So this isn’t about condemnation.
It’s about invitation.
An invitation back to God’s design.
Back to wholeness.
Back to a kind of love that doesn’t leave you in pieces.
Because He isn’t.
Not even close.
And if this stirred something in you… don’t keep it to yourself.
Because this is bigger than information.
This is transformation.
And if you truly want to glorify God… support what is feeding your spirit.
There’s something powerful about standing behind truth that convicts, restores, and points people back to Jesus.
Because the question was never “Why does God restrict sex?”
The real question is…
Why would we settle for less than what He designed it to be?
And maybe tonight…
You finally stop calling broken things normal.
